Using scalar dipole–dipole coupling for the two induced dipoles,
\[
\mathbf p_i=\alpha_i\mathbf E_i(\mathbf r_i),
\]
the interaction energy in the far field \(kd_0\gg1\) is
\[
U_{\rm int}\simeq
-\frac{k^2\alpha_1\alpha_2E_1E_2}{4\pi\epsilon_0d_0}
\cos\!\left[k(z_1-z_2)+\Phi\right],
\qquad
\Phi=\phi_1-\phi_2+\frac{z_1^2-z_2^2}{2z_R}.
\]
Here the Gaussian-beam phase is
\[
\psi_i(z_i)=kz_i-\phi_i-\arctan(z_i/z_R),
\]
so the relative propagation phase along \(z\) is
\[
k(z_1-z_2)-(\phi_1-\phi_2)
-\arctan(z_1/z_R)+\arctan(z_2/z_R).
\]
For \(z_1,z_2\ll z_R\),
\[
\arctan(z_i/z_R)\simeq z_i/z_R,
\]
and the quadratic term in the interaction must be combined with the trap curvature term; this gives the longitudinal equilibrium condition. Expanding the interaction force about that equilibrium gives, to leading order in \(1/(kd_0)\),
\[
F_1^{(\mathrm{int})}
=-\frac{k^3\alpha_1\alpha_2E_1E_2}{4\pi\epsilon_0d_0}
\left(1+\frac{z_1+z_2}{2kz_R}\right)
\sin\!\left[k(z_1-z_2)+\Phi\right].
\]
Linearizing in the small relative displacement yields
\[
F_1^{(\mathrm{int})}\simeq
-(k_1+k_2)(z_1-z_2),\qquad
F_2^{(\mathrm{int})}\simeq
-(k_1-k_2)(z_2-z_1),
\]
with
\[
k_1=
\frac{k^4\alpha_1\alpha_2E_1E_2}{4\pi\epsilon_0d_0}
\sin\!\left(\phi_1-\phi_2\right),
\]
and
\[
k_2=
\frac{k^3\alpha_1\alpha_2E_1E_2}{8\pi\epsilon_0z_Rd_0}
\cos\!\left(\phi_1-\phi_2\right).
\]
Thus \(k_1\) is the reciprocal optical-binding spring, while \(k_2\) is the nonreciprocal contribution arising from the axial intensity/phase gradient of the Gaussian beams.

\[

Let \(g_{ij}(\rho)=\gamma_{ij}(x,\rho)\), and write
\[
g^{(m)}_{ij}=\left.\partial_\rho^{\,m}g_{ij}\right|_{\rho=0}.
\]
The factorials are important because the expansion in the question uses unnormalized Taylor coefficients:
\[
\gamma^{(m)}_{ij}=\frac1{m!}g^{(m)}_{ij}.
\]

For the ambient metric in normal form, Ricci-flatness gives
\[
g'_{ij}=2P_{ij},
\]
and the next two determined coefficients can be written as
\[
\frac12 g''_{ij}
=\Omega^{(1)}_{ij}+P_i{}^kP_{kj},
\]
\[
\frac12 g'''_{ij}
=\Omega^{(2)}_{ij}
+4P^k{}_{(i}\Omega^{(1)}_{j)k}.
\]
Consequently,
\[
\gamma^{(2)}_{ij}
=\Omega^{(1)}_{ij}+P_i{}^kP_{kj},
\]
and
\[
\gamma^{(3)}_{ij}
=\frac13\Omega^{(2)}_{ij}
+\frac43 P^k{}_{(i}\Omega^{(1)}_{j)k}.
\]

Since \(P_i{}^kP_{kj}\) is regular at \(d=4\), while \(P\Omega^{(1)}\) has no pole at \(d=6\), the residue-matching constants are
\[
A_2=1,\qquad A_3=\frac13.
\]

Using the standard Fefferman–Graham convention
\[
\Omega^{(1)}_{ij}=\frac{1}{4-d}B_{ij},
\]
the second difference becomes
\[
\gamma^{(3)}_{ij}-\frac13\Omega^{(2)}_{ij}
=\frac{4}{3(4-d)}B_{k(i}P^k{}_{j)}.
\]
On the \(d=6\) pole hypersurface, this coefficient is \(-2/3\).

Thus, with unit-weight symmetrization,
\[
\boxed{
\begin{aligned}
A_2&=1,
&
\gamma^{(2)}_{ij}-\Omega^{(1)}_{ij}
&=P_i{}^kP_{kj},
\\[2mm]
A_3&=\frac13,
&
\gamma^{(3)}_{ij}-\frac13\Omega^{(2)}_{ij}
&=\frac{4}{3(4-d)}B_{k(i}P^k{}_{j)}
\;\overset{d=6}{=}\;
-\frac23\,B_{k(i}P^k{}_{j)} .
\end{aligned}}
\]

Let the normalized variables be
\[
z=\log_2 t,\qquad \varphi=\log_2\ell(t).
\]
At the marginal exponent \(\mu=2\), the long-range-dispersal self-consistency balance gives
\[
\ell(t)\sim \frac{2K}{\ln 2}\,\frac{t}{\ln t}.
\]
Therefore
\[
\varphi
=\log_2\ell(t)
=\log_2 t-\log_2\ln t+\log_2\!\left(\frac{2K}{\ln 2}\right)+o(1).
\]
Since \(\ln t=z\ln 2\),
\[
\log_2\ln t=\log_2 z+\log_2\ln 2.
\]
The last logarithm is constant, so it can be absorbed into the ignored constant term. Hence, retaining all nonconstant terms through constant order,
\[
\boxed{\varphi(z)=z-\log_2 z+O(1)}.
\]

Strictly, the integral equation printed in the prompt has no time derivative; the marginal \(t/\ln t\) correction assumes the standard Hallatschek–Fisher self-consistency equation, whose convolution contains \(\dot\ell(\tau)\ell(t-\tau)\).

For the Werner shield,
\[
d_{\mathrm{sym}}=\frac{d(d+1)}{2},\qquad
d_{\mathrm{asym}}=\frac{d(d-1)}{2}.
\]
At \(q=(d+1)/(2d)\), both weights become equal:
\[
\frac{q}{d_{\mathrm{sym}}}
=\frac{1-q}{d_{\mathrm{asym}}}
=\frac1{d^2}.
\]
For the corresponding private channel, the maximal one-copy coherent information is then \(1/d\). The Spin Alignment Conjecture supplies the entropy minimization needed to prove additivity, giving for every \(n\),
\[
\mathcal Q^{(1)}(\mathcal N^{\otimes n})=n\mathcal Q^{(1)}(\mathcal N)
=\frac nd.
\]
Hence the regularized quantum capacity is single-letter and equals
\[
\boxed{\mathcal Q(\mathcal N)=\frac1d}
\]
in qubits per channel use, assuming base-2 logarithms.

At \(n=1\), the prescribed interpolation gives
\[
Z_{\mathrm{can}}(1,\eta)=\int_0^1\vartheta_\eta(t)\,dt=1.
\]
Therefore,
\[
\left.\frac{\partial Z_{\mathrm{can}}}{\partial n}\right|_{n=1}
=
\frac12-\frac12\ln\eta+
\int_0^1\vartheta_\eta(t)\ln\vartheta_\eta(t)\,dt,
\]
so the subtracted prefactor cancels:
\[
F(\eta)=\int_0^1\vartheta_\eta(t)\ln\vartheta_\eta(t)\,dt.
\]

Using the Poisson-dual form
\[
\vartheta_\eta(t)=\sqrt{\eta}\sum_{m\in\mathbb Z}
e^{-\pi\eta(t-m)^2},
\]
and evaluating the rapidly convergent integral at \(\eta=10\pi/3\) gives
\[
F\!\left(\frac{10\pi}{3}\right)
=0.674499120060534613125348547361304374991\ldots
\]

\[
\boxed{F\!\left(\frac{10\pi}{3}\right)\approx 0.67449912}
\]

**Calculation**
- SI dark-electric amplitude:  
  \[
  E_D=\sqrt{\frac{2\rho}{\epsilon_0}}
      =3.8047\times10^3\ {\rm V\,m^{-1}},
  \]
  using \(\rho=0.4\,{\rm GeV\,cm^{-3}}=6.4087\times10^{-5}\,{\rm J\,m^{-3}}\).
- At \(f=250\) Hz and \(v=230\,{\rm km\,s^{-1}}\),
  \[
  \tau=\frac{1}{f(v/c)^2}=6.7959\times10^3\ {\rm s},\qquad
  T_{\rm eff}=\sqrt{\tau T}=1.6697\times10^6\ {\rm s}.
  \]
  Hence the SNR-one power threshold is
  \[
  \sqrt{\langle h^2\rangle}_{\rm th}
  =\sqrt{\frac{S_h}{T_{\rm eff}}}
  =\frac{3\times10^{-24}}{\sqrt{T_{\rm eff}}}
  =2.3217\times10^{-27}.
  \]
- Writing \(\theta=2\pi fL/c=0.0209296\), \(\beta=v/c\), and
  \[
  I=1-\cos\theta\,{\rm sinc}(\theta\beta)
   =2.19017\times10^{-4},
  \]
  the polarization/propagation-averaged response is
  \[
  \langle h^2\rangle
  =\epsilon_{B-L}^2
   \left(\frac{eE_D}{m_n\omega^2L}\right)^2
   \frac23\left[\delta q^2+2(0.5)(0.5+\delta q)I\right],
  \]
  with
  \[
  \frac{eE_D}{m_n\omega^2L}=36.9265.
  \]
  The first term is the added-doping response; the second is the retained undoped finite-light-time/spatial-gradient response.

Solving \(\langle h^2\rangle=S_h/T_{\rm eff}\) gives
\[
\boxed{
\epsilon_{B-L}^{\min}(250\,{\rm Hz})\simeq
\begin{cases}
1.03\times10^{-27}, & \delta q=0.074,\\[2mm]
6.35\times10^{-27}, & \delta q=6\times10^{-3},\\[2mm]
7.35\times10^{-27}, & \delta q=5\times10^{-4}.
\end{cases}}
\]

For \(\delta q=5\times10^{-4}\), the retained undoped finite-light-time contribution dominates, so the reach approaches the undoped floor \(7.36\times10^{-27}\).

40.response:
For plane waves \(n,\theta\propto e^{ikx-i\omega t}\), the linearized Josephson relation is
\[
\partial_t\theta+\mu=0,\qquad \mu=\frac{n}{\chi}.
\]
Quadrupole conservation gives the linearized mode equation
\[
\chi\,\omega^2+i\sigma k^4\omega-\kappa k^6=0.
\]
Solving the quadratic gives
\[
\boxed{
\omega_\pm(k)
=
-\frac{i\sigma}{2\chi}k^4
\pm |k|^3
\sqrt{\frac{\kappa}{\chi}
-\frac{\sigma^2}{4\chi^2}k^2}
}
\]
with the convention \(e^{-i\omega t}\), so positive \(\sigma\) gives damping. At long wavelength,
\[
\omega_\pm(k)=\pm\sqrt{\frac{\kappa}{\chi}}\,|k|^3
-\frac{i\sigma}{2\chi}k^4+\mathcal O(k^5),
\]
so the two hydrodynamic modes are a quadrupole-superfluid pair with cubic dispersion and quartic attenuation.

\]

A single-arm collinear solution is therefore forced into the alternating \(z\)-column arrangement \((m_z,-m_z)\). With both \(q_1\) and \(q_2\) present, relative amplitudes leave three possible invariant/arithmetic classes.

The optical constraints then eliminate the higher-symmetry alternatives:

- Birefringence excludes a surviving trigonal magnetic lattice.
- Magneto-optic Kerr excludes any mesoscale inversion-containing candidate, including the trigonal orbit alternatives.
- The surviving classes are the orthorhombic \(Pca2_1\) subgroup, the monoclinic \(P2_1\) subgroup, and the triclinic \(P1\) subgroup.

Thus, in ascending BNS-number order, all possibilities are

\[
\boxed{182.151,\quad 182.152,\quad 182.153}
\]

29.response:
Assume the two standing-wave pairs form the usual phase-controlled square lattice, with no residual cross-interference between the \(x\) and \(y\) pairs. Define

\[
k=\frac{2\pi}{\lambda},\qquad
E_R=\frac{\hbar^2k^2}{2m},\qquad
s=\frac{V_0}{E_R},
\]

where \(V_0\) is the depth of either one-dimensional standing-wave lattice. With the convention \(V_{\rm dip}=-\alpha|\mathcal E|^2/2\) and complex beam amplitude \(E\), one has \(V_0=2|\alpha||E|^2\).

Near a lattice minimum,

\[
V\simeq \text{const}
+\frac{m\omega^2}{2}(x^2+y^2)
+\frac{m\omega_z^2}{2}z^2,
\]

with, for \(W\gg\lambda\),

\[
\omega=\frac{2\sqrt{V_0E_R}}{\hbar},\qquad
\omega_z=\sqrt{\frac{8V_0}{mW^2}}.
\]

Thus the Gaussian Wannier orbital has oscillator lengths

\[
\ell_x=\ell_y=\ell=\frac{1}{k s^{1/4}},\qquad
\ell_z=\sqrt{\frac{W}{2k}}\,s^{-1/4}.
\]

Using \(g=4\pi\hbar^2a_s/m\) and

\[
U=g\int d^3r\,|w(\mathbf r)|^4
=\frac{g}{(2\pi)^{3/2}\ell_x\ell_y\ell_z},
\]

gives the on-site interaction below. For tunneling, neighboring Gaussian orbitals have overlap
\(S=e^{-\pi^2\sqrt{s}/4}\). After Löwdin orthogonalization,

\[
\frac{t_{\rm HO}}{E_R}
=
\frac{s\left(\frac{\pi^2}{4}-e^{-1/\sqrt{s}}\right)e^{-\pi^2\sqrt{s}/4}}
{1-e^{-\pi^2\sqrt{s}/2}}
\simeq
\left(\frac{\pi^2}{4}-1\right)s e^{-\pi^2\sqrt{s}/4}.
\]

Gaussian tails underestimate barrier penetration; the standard deep-sinusoidal-lattice Mathieu result is also shown.

\[
\boxed{
\begin{aligned}
t_{\rm HO}
&\simeq
E_R\left(\frac{\pi^2}{4}-1\right)
s\,e^{-\pi^2\sqrt{s}/4}
\\[2mm]
&=
E_R\left(\frac{\pi^2}{4}-1\right)
\left(\frac{2|\alpha||E|^2}{E_R}\right)
\exp\!\left[
-\frac{\pi^2}{4}
\sqrt{\frac{2|\alpha||E|^2}{E_R}}
\right],
\\[3mm]
t_{\rm deep\ sinusoid}
&\simeq
\frac{4}{\sqrt{\pi}}E_R\,s^{3/4}e^{-2\sqrt{s}}
\\[2mm]
&=
\frac{4}{\sqrt{\pi}}E_R
\left(\frac{2|\alpha||E|^2}{E_R}\right)^{3/4}
\exp\!\left[
-2\sqrt{\frac{2|\alpha||E|^2}{E_R}}
\right],
\\[3mm]
U
&\simeq
\frac{4}{\sqrt{\pi}}E_R\,
\frac{k a_s}{\sqrt{kW}}\,s^{3/4}
\\[2mm]
&=
\frac{4}{\sqrt{\pi}}E_R
\left(\frac{2\pi a_s}{\lambda}\right)
\sqrt{\frac{\lambda}{2\pi W}}
\left(\frac{2|\alpha||E|^2}{E_R}\right)^{3/4}.
\end{aligned}}
\]

Here \(U\) assumes two distinguishable spin components; identical spin-polarized fermions have no \(s\)-wave contact interaction. If all four beams are mutually coherent with the same phase, their cross-interference produces a rotated checkerboard lattice and changes the numerical factors.

Using the convention in the question, let \(q_{\mu\nu}=P_{\mu\nu}/(d-2)\) denote the standard Schouten tensor. In \(d=8\), the obstruction/Bach basis is related to the displayed tensor by
\[
B_{\mu\nu}=4\,q_{\mu\nu}^2-2q_{\mu\rho}q^\rho{}_\nu ,
\qquad
B^{\mu\nu}q_{\mu\nu}
=\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{tr}(P^3)-\frac{1}{18}\operatorname{tr}(P^2)\operatorname{tr}(P).
\]
Consequently,
\[
\operatorname{tr}(B^2)
=4\operatorname{tr}(P^4)-\frac{8}{3}\operatorname{tr}(P^3)\operatorname{tr}(P)
+\frac{4}{9}\bigl(\operatorname{tr}P^2\bigr)^2,
\]
and the \(O\)-terms simplify to
\[
\frac1{192}\operatorname{tr}(OP)+\frac1{48}\operatorname{tr}(OP^2)
=\frac1{1728}\operatorname{tr}(P^4).
\]

Starting from the \(d=8\) Q-curvature expression
\[
Q_8=
\frac18\operatorname{tr}(q^4)
-\frac16\operatorname{tr}(q^3)\operatorname{tr}(q)
-\frac1{16}\bigl(\operatorname{tr}q^2\bigr)^2
+\frac18\operatorname{tr}(q^2)(\operatorname{tr}q)^2
-\frac1{48}(\operatorname{tr}q)^4
+\frac1{24}\operatorname{tr}(Bq)
+\frac1{384}\operatorname{tr}(B^2),
\]
and substituting \(q=P/6\), the nonvanishing coefficients in
\[
\mathcal A_4=-\frac{L^7}{8\pi G}\int d^8x\,
\sqrt{-\det\gamma^{(0)}}\,X^{(4)}\ln\mathcal B
\]
are therefore
\[
\boxed{
\begin{aligned}
X^{(4)}={}&
-\frac{1}{7776}\,\operatorname{tr}(P^3)\operatorname{tr}(P)
-\frac{1}{20736}\,\bigl(\operatorname{tr}P^2\bigr)^2
+\frac{1}{10368}\,\operatorname{tr}(P^2)(\operatorname{tr}P)^2
-\frac{1}{62208}\,(\operatorname{tr}P)^4
\\[2mm]
&+\frac{1}{864}\,\operatorname{tr}(BP)
+\frac{1}{1728}\,\operatorname{tr}(P^4).
\end{aligned}}
\]

Thus the coefficient table is
\[
\boxed{
\begin{array}{c|r}
\text{term} & \text{coefficient}\\ \hline
\operatorname{tr}(P^4) & \dfrac{1}{1728}\\
\operatorname{tr}(P^3) & 0\\
\operatorname{tr}(P^3)\operatorname{tr}(P) & -\dfrac{1}{7776}\\
\operatorname{tr}(BP) & \dfrac{1}{864}\\
\operatorname{tr}(BP^2) & 0\\
\operatorname{tr}(B^2) & 0\\
\operatorname{tr}(B^2P) & 0\\
\operatorname{tr}(OP) & 0\\
\operatorname{tr}(OP^2) & 0\\
\operatorname{tr}(\Omega) & 0\\
\operatorname{tr}(\Omega P) & 0\\
(\operatorname{tr}P^2)^2 & -\dfrac{1}{20736}\\
\operatorname{tr}(P^2)(\operatorname{tr}P)^2 & \dfrac{1}{10368}\\
(\operatorname{tr}P)^4 & -\dfrac{1}{62208}\\
\operatorname{tr}(BP)\operatorname{tr}(P) & 0
\end{array}}
\]

Tracking the transmitted ray through the plate (glass path \(nl/\cos\theta\) after subtracting the vacuum segment the plate displaces) gives the single-crossing optical-path response
\[
\delta W=\Big(\tfrac{n}{\cos\theta}-\tfrac{1+\tan\theta}{\sqrt2}\Big)\delta l
+\Big[\tfrac{1}{\cos\theta}\big(1-\tan^2\theta\big)+\tfrac{\sec^2\theta\tan\theta}{n\sqrt2}\Big]\,l\,\delta n ,
\]
while the reflected arm samples the front-surface displacement \(\delta l/(2\sqrt2)\). Round-trips double the transmitted contribution, so
\[
\delta(L_x-L_y)_{\rm opt}=2\,\delta W+\frac{\delta l}{2\sqrt2}.
\]
With the fixed values \(\delta l/l=-\delta\alpha/\alpha\), \(\delta n/n=-0.0442\,\delta\alpha/\alpha\), \(\delta m_e=0\), both terms have the same sign:
\[

=6.11080\,l\,\delta\alpha/\alpha=0.36665\,m\,\cdot\,\delta\alpha/\alpha .
\]
